title: BEYOND BLACK OCTOBER: AN AI-DRIVEN PREDICTIVE CYBER DEFENSE FRAMEWORK FOR PREVENTING AUTONOMOUS EXPLOITATION OF CRITICAL SOFTWARE VULNERABILITIES
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming cybersecurity by enabling automated vulnerability discovery, exploit development, threat analysis, and defensive security operations. However, these capabilities also introduce significa nt risks when sophisticated AI systems are used to identify and exploit weaknesses in widely deployed software. The October 2026 PHP security crisis, commonly described in media coverage as Black October, illustrates this emerging security challenge. Two c ritical vulnerabilities, CVE - 2026 - 109618 and CVE - 2026 - 109619, affected the PHP runtime and created opportunities for unauthenticated remote code execution. The vulnerabilities were addressed through security releases on October 21, 2026, following AI - assis ted discovery involving Wiz Research and Google's Gemini technology. This research examines the relationship between advanced AI - assisted vulnerability discovery and the growing speed of automated cyber exploitation. It investigates the technical characteristics of the PHP vulnerabilities, the limitations of conventional vu lnerability management, the operational challenges facing small and medium - sized organizations, and the implications of autonomous AI agents for global cybersecurity. The paper proposes an AI - Driven Predictive Cyber Defense Framework (AIPCDF), a multilayer security architecture integrating AI - assisted vulnerability assessment, software dependency intelligence, continuous attack - surface monitoring, behavioral anomaly det ection, automated patch prioritization, zero - trust access controls, and human - supervised incident response. The proposed framework emphasizes preventive security rather than relying exclusively on emergency patching after public disclosure. A conceptual research methodology is developed to evaluate the proposed framework using vulnerability detection accuracy, mean time to remediation, false - positive rates, exploit detection latency, and recovery performance. The paper does not claim experime ntal validation; instead, it establishes a reproducible evaluation design for future implementation. The findings from the case analysis suggest that the next generation of cybersecurity must combine secure software engineering, responsible AI deployment, automated threat intelligence, and organizational resilience. The proposed framework offers a practic al direction for protecting critical digital infrastructure against increasingly capable AI - assisted cyber threats.
authors: Ashikur Rahman
venue: International Journal of Engineering Technology Research & Management

title: Self-Operating Code Refactoring and Vulnerability Detection Using Static Analysis and Machine Learning Models
abstract: Modern enterprise software development faces unprecedented challenges due to the rapid accumulation of technical debt and security vulnerabilities. Traditional static application security testing (SAST) tools suffer from high false-positive rates and lack automated remediation capabilities. Conversely, pure machine learning (ML) models often generate syntactically incorrect code or fail to ensure program semantic equivalence during refactoring. This paper proposes AutoRefact-Sec, an autonomous, self-operating hybrid framework that unifies deterministic static analysis with probabilistic Transformer-based Deep Learning models. By combining Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) representation, Control Flow Graphs (CFG), and Data Flow Graphs (DFG) with a fine-tuned Graph Neural Network (GNN) and CodeBERT backend, AutoRefact-Sec achieves real-time vulnerability detection (CWE identification) and performs context-aware, safety-guaranteed code refactoring without human intervention. We evaluate our framework on a dataset of 150,000 open-source C/C++ and Java functions. Experimental results indicate a 94.2% precision rate in vulnerability detection and an 88.6% success rate in autonomous refactoring validation via symbolic execution and automated regression testing.
authors: Sachin Sharma
venue: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews

title: How much model does warning triage need? A cost-aware comparison from rules to locally run language models
abstract: Static analysis tools report far more warnings than developers act on, and machine learning is widely proposed to identify the actionable ones. Published comparisons rarely include a simple label-based reference, and rarely report quality on unseen projects together with compute time. This study compares five levels of model complexity on two open datasets, NASCAR (Java) and AW4C (C): a warning-type prior, a linear model on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features, a frozen code encoder, fine-tuned code encoders, and open-weight large language models (LLMs) run locally. All models were scored on the same 1,000 warnings per dataset and protocol, using the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) with project-level bootstrap intervals. Three findings emerged. First, in the original AW4C release the number of lines in the supplied code context predicted the label with an MCC of 0.91 on unseen projects, and fine-tuned CodeBERT reached 0.81; in a variant rebuilt with a uniform context window, which also differs in composition, the corresponding values were 0.12 and 0.30. Second, on unseen NASCAR projects an advantage of fine-tuned encoders over the warning-type prior was not established: the paired difference in MCC was −0.08 (95% CI −0.21 to 0.02) for CodeBERT. Third, locally run LLMs without task-specific training scored near zero on NASCAR with the default threshold and required about 47 times the mean processing time of a fine-tuned encoder. Model complexity should be assessed against a simple reference under cross-project evaluation.
authors: Peter Sullivan; Bogdan Mikhaylov

title: MOS: Towards Effective Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection through Mixture-of-Experts Tuning of Large Language Models
abstract: Smart contract vulnerabilities pose significant security risks to blockchain systems, potentially leading to severe financial losses. Existing methods face several limitations: (1) Program analysis-based approaches heavily rely on predefined patterns, lacking flexibility and adaptability to new vulnerability types; (2) Deep learning-based methods lack explanations for their detection results; (3) Large language model-based approaches suffer from high false positive rates. To address these challenges, we propose MOS, a smart contract vulnerability detection framework based on mixture-of-experts tuning (MOE-Tuning) of large language models. First, we conduct Continual Pre-training on a large-scale smart contract dataset to provide a domain-enhanced initialization for the subsequent MOE-Tuning process. Second, to provide reliable explanations for detected vulnerabilities, we construct a high-quality MOE-Tuning dataset through a multi-stage pipeline combining large language model generation and expert verification. Third, we design a vulnerability-aware routing mechanism that activates the most relevant expert networks by analyzing code features and their matching degree with experts, addressing the limitation of predefined patterns in program analysis approaches. Finally, we extend the feed-forward layers of the LLM after Continual Pre-training into multiple parallel expert networks, each specializing in specific vulnerability patterns. We also employ a dual-objective loss function: one for optimizing vulnerability detection and explanation performance, and another for balancing expert utilization through an auxiliary loss based on the scaled dot product of expert assignment frequencies and average routing probabilities, thereby improving model performance in complex vulnerability scenarios. Extensive experiments show that MOS consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in four foundational and historically significant vulnerability types (Reentrancy, Timestamp, Integer Overflow/Underflow, Delegatecall) with average improvements of 6.38% in F1 score and 4.84% in accuracy. The vulnerability explanations generated by MOS also demonstrate high quality, achieving positive ratings (scores of 3 and 4 on a 4-point scale) of 82.96%, 85.21% and 94.58% for correctness, completeness, and conciseness, respectively, through a combined approach of human evaluation and LLM evaluation. Extensibility experiments show that MOS effectively handles new vulnerability types (Access Control, Price Oracle Manipulation, Logic Errors, Lack of Input Validation, Slippage, and Risky First Deposit), consistently outperforming all baseline methods across six additional vulnerability categories. MOS achieved an average F1 score of 83.94% and an average accuracy of 87.82%, demonstrating its strong extensibility and flexibility in handling new vulnerabilities.
authors: Hang Yuan; Lei Yu; Zhirong Huang; Jingyuan Zhang; Junyi Lu; Shiqiang Cheng; Li Yang; Fengjun Zhang; Jiajia Ma; Chun Zuo
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

title: Beyond Compilation Feedback: Refining Vulnerability Checkers with Program-Analysis Evidence
abstract: Recent work shows that LLMs can synthesize static-analysis checkers from security patches, but a compilable checker is not necessarily a correct one. A patch reveals what changed, not why the change is safe, so generated checkers often match only the surface edit and miss the deeper semantic condition. Existing refinement loops feed back compilation errors and validation reports, yet these signals describe symptoms without explaining what the checker misunderstands about the code. We observe that the analysis framework itself already computes the information needed to close this gap. Control-flow graphs, symbolic values, memory regions and checker callbacks are available inside the analyzer but unused by current refinement strategies. SemWeaver is a plug-in refinement layer that extracts patch-relevant analyzer evidence and assembles it with source context and validation feedback into a structured, provenance-labelled bundle. An iterative editing loop refines the checker on both the vulnerable and fixed revisions, guarded by a retention gate that accepts warning recovery or false-positive reduction while preventing over-pruning. We evaluate SemWeaver on 39 KNighter-derived CSA checkers from Linux kernel fixes. With analyzer evidence, refinement reaches 23 warning-positive vulnerable revisions (vs. 15 for KNighter's loop) and raises version-level $F_1$ from 0.448 to 0.575. An ablation removing internal evidence recovers fewer silent cases and produces different checker edits, indicating that the two evidence configurations address complementary recognition gaps. Additional experiments cover three editor models on a 12-subject subset, a CodeQL query refinement, and controlled source-form variations. A qualitative follow-up on all 11 non-tied comparisons traces each warning-count change to a specific checker repair, such as recognizing a lowered callback or unwrapping an expression cast.
authors: Cheng-Zhi Yi; Shen-Ao Wang; Yan-Jie Zhao; Xiao Cheng; Hao-Yu Wang

title: An empirical lifecycle security validation framework for web application development and deployment
abstract: Web applications remain vulnerable to cyberattacks such as SQL Injection (SQLi), Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Command Injection, insecure container deployments, and software supply-chain attacks. Although modern DevSecOps practices integrate security throughout software development, existing security mechanisms often address these issues independently and provide limited support for systematic lifecycle security validation. This study presents an empirically validated lifecycle security methodology that integrates secure coding practices, container security, software supply-chain verification, deployment verification, and runtime monitoring into a unified software engineering workflow. The proposed methodology was implemented and experimentally evaluated using a purposely vulnerable Flask web application. The security effectiveness was verified through vulnerability assessments, secure coding, automated static security analyses, container hardening, software supply-chain verification, and runtime attack detection. The experimental findings show that all four representative application-layer attack attempts were prevented under the controlled experimental conditions, resulting in an Attack Prevention Rate (APR) of 100% (4/4). The container hardening process reduced the number of vulnerabilities identified from 1067 to 53 (VRR = 95.0%). In addition, the deployment validation satisfied all seven predefined security requirements (DCR = 100%) under the evaluated experimental conditions. These results demonstrate that integrating lifecycle security validation into software development and deployment workflows provides a practical and reproducible methodology for improving web application security while supporting modern secure software engineering and DevSecOps practices.
authors: Gonesh Chandra Saha; Ahmed Afif Monrat; Ahmed Afif Monrat

title: Implementation of an Effective Code Vulnerability Detection Model Using Deep Learning and Attention Mechanism
abstract: With increasing computational power, deep learning methods have been widely applied to software vulnerability detection. Compared to traditional machine learning, deep learning offers low computational overhead, high accuracy, and eliminates the need for manual feature engineering. However, many existing approaches lack sufficient utilization of code syntax and semantics, limiting performance. This study proposes VDDA (Vulnerability Detection based on Deep learning and Attention mechanisms), an effective model that combines deep learning with attention mechanisms. VDDA employs a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BLSTM) network to capture code features automatically. Source code is transformed into Code Property Graphs (CPG) using the Joern tool to retain rich syntactic and semantic information. To enhance feature representation, several strategies are applied: depth-first traversal-based CPG optimization, three-directional code slicing, code block-based slice organization, and separation of function and variable names during symbolization. These methods convert source code into vector representations suitable as input to the deep model. An attention mechanism is integrated with BLSTM to emphasize the most relevant parts of the input vectors for improved vulnerability detection. Experiments on two datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that VDDA achieves superior detection performance compared to existing methods, validating its effectiveness and generalizability in software vulnerability detection tasks.
authors: Erzhou Zhu; Le-Hao Qi; Jia-Qi Chang; Zhu-juan Ma

title: When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
abstract: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.
authors: Artur ZIEBA-KOZARZEWSKI; Bartosz Grzegorzewski

title: APG: Agentic Static-Analysis Infrastructure on LLVM-IR Graph Databases
abstract: LLM-based coding agents increasingly rely on external program knowledge, yet access to static-analysis graphs alone does not ensure appropriate operation selection or evidence interpretation. We present APG, an infrastructure for semantics-grounded static program analysis. Built on SVF and LLVM, it decomposes compiler-derived program analyses into atomic capabilities that LLM agents can select, compose, and orchestrate for goal-directed, cross-graph investigation, with query safeguards and evidence traces preserving inspectable results and provenance. APG provides 38 atomic capabilities. On analysis requests arising during benchmark repair runs, 35 achieve first-attempt query-generation success rates above 50%, including 13 at 100%. Evaluation on 812 C/C++ defects shows higher repair success than the evaluated baselines. Compared with Passive Graph Push, APG improves first-iteration repair success by 17.6 and 18.0 percentage points on the two benchmark collections and reduces average LLM input-token consumption by 90.8%. Our tool is available at https://github.com/JasonZhongZexin/APG-ICSE-Demo and its demonstration video at https://youtu.be/vkuExZUjGnw
authors: Zexin Zhong; Yanjun Zhang; Yulei Sui; Xiao Cheng

title: StateGate: A Behavioral-Fidelity Prompt Optimization Method for Long-Chain LLM Agents
abstract: Currently, long-chain LLM agents commonly suffer from behavioral degradation in complex tasks, where prompts are written in full but steps are not executed in full. To address this issue, existing approaches face three major challenges. First, constraints are strongly bound to their textual carriers; once natural-language constraint sentences are removed, their binding force vanishes. Second, the execution process lacks independent verification, as the evidence for judgment is often supplied by the executing party itself, leading to the failure of self-referential validation. Third, existing remediation schemes are difficult to generalize, and hard-coded mechanisms cannot be transferred across tasks. In this paper, we propose StateGate, a novel prompt-optimization scheme that transforms semantic constraints into symbolic gates enforced by an external deterministic runtime. By decoupling the content of a constraint from its carrier of efficacy, StateGate achieves behavioral fidelity in long-chain tasks without losing the binding force of the prompt. Specifically, we first propose four independent compression strategies (deduplication, generalization, externalization, and text-to-gating) together with their corresponding decision chains, enabling principled prompt symbolization. Second, we design a three-component architecture consisting of a state file, a validator, and an orchestrator, which thoroughly separates judgment authority from execution authority. Third, we formally prove that the compliance of symbolic constraints is independent of context size. Finally, we validate the framework on a vulnerability-discovery task in the security domain; the results show that StateGate achieves 100% execution closure and accurate vulnerability detection.
authors: Shicheng Huang; Cai Fu; Lyu Jianqiang; Yifan Zhang; Xianmao Ji

title: Blockchain-Enabled Zero Trust Architecture for Securing Cloud Computing based on Cybersecurity Risk Auditing Framework
abstract: Traditional cloud security controls tend to treat access, vulnerability exposure, and audit integrity as distinct functions, reducing the ability to be aware of risks on an ongoing basis. In this study, the authors present a blockchain-based zero-trust risk auditing framework for adaptive cloud protection (ACP) called BAZTRA. BAZTRA is a combination of a GBDT-based network-risk estimator and identity, device-posture, provenance, vulnerability, and compliance evidence. The CICIoT2023 corpus, controlled contextual replay, and repeated ten-seed experiments were used to evaluate the following techniques: availability-aware fusion, temporal smoothing, four-state enforcement, EPSS-KEV prioritization, hash chaining, and Merkle-based audit anchoring. Statistical significance was assessed using Friedman and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests across repetitions. The selected network-risk estimator achieved 78.96% accuracy, 55.01% macro-F1, 0.964 ROC-AUC, and 0.718 MCC. The complete BAZTRA framework produced 89.44% decision macro-F1, reduced unsafe access to 0.67%, and limited false denial to 0.03%. Ablation confirmed that adaptive enforcement, network evidence, provenance analysis, and availability-aware normalization were the most influential components. Merkle batching reduced effective ledger payload by 98.21% while preserving detection of modification, deletion, reordering, and replay attempts. BAZTRA provides a unified approach to continuous access assessment, vulnerability prioritization, and accountable cloud auditing. Future work will validate the framework on complete multi-source telemetry and a physical multi-peer Hyperledger Fabric deployment.
authors: Mohammed Amin Almaiah; Santosh Reddy Addula
venue: Jordanian Journal of Informatics and Computing

title: The Dual-Use Nature of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity: A Bibliometric Analysis and Critical Review
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) now occupy three positions in cybersecurity at once: they are systems that must be secured, capabilities that lower the cost of offence, and instruments that augment defence. Existing reviews typically examine one of these roles in isolation, which obscures how the roles interact and leaves the field without an evidence base for judging whether the interactions are being studied. This article addresses that gap by combining a VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis with a critical literature review. We retrieved 13,756 records published between January 2023 and 19 October 2026 from OpenAlex and, after document-type, language, abstract, de-duplication and validated relevance screening (precision 84.0%, 95% CI 78.3–88.4%), analysed 7,369 documents through performance analysis, keyword co-occurrence and co-citation mapping in VOSviewer and a dictionary-based classification of each document's dual-use role. The co-occurrence map resolves into four thematic clusters: attacks on and alignment of LLMs; LLM-enabled detection and security operations; code and vulnerability analysis, including penetration testing; and socio-technical threats and governance. Research on LLMs as targets (42.8% of documents) and as defensive tools (35.3%) has grown largely in parallel: only 7.9% of documents address more than one role, and only 11.1% of defensive studies engage with attacks on the defending model itself, falling to 2.5% for vulnerability detection. The critical review explains why this matters: reported success rates of offensive LLM agents range from 0% to 90% depending on experimental design, few defences are evaluated against adaptive adversaries, and the security–utility trade-off is rarely quantified. We formalise these findings in a coupled dual-use framework with three testable propositions and derive eight research directions, prioritising adaptive evaluation, multilingual guardrail robustness, longitudinal measurement and the security of defensive LLM deployments.
authors: Muhammad Sharjeel Aziz; Muhammad Ali; Adnan R. Manzoor; Muhammad Younis; Zulfiya Khabirova

title: Set an Exploit to Catch an Exploit: Compiling Public Proofs of Concept into Threat Hunting Rules
abstract: Public exploit code for a newly disclosed vulnerability usually appears before any published rule that detects its exploitation. Of the 45 CVEs we evaluate, 37 ever received a Sigma, Elastic or Splunk rule; in 33 the exploit came first, by a median of 22 days. Analysts still write every rule by hand. We present Encore, which compiles a public Python proof-of-concept exploit (PoC) into CVE-specific hunting rules over a web service's existing logs, without running it. Encore rests on the PoC Behavior Alignment Principle: a PoC performs the exploit, so its code already provides a rule's HTTP requests, payloads and host operations. That is hard to act on: a PoC is written against libraries and runs on the attacker's machine, while the target's web-server, proxy and host logs record only what arrived and what it did. Encore closes the gap with a map from library calls to the operations they cause, built once per library, keeping only the operations visible on the target. For 12 of the 45, Encore's rule states the exploit's own payload fragment or host operation, which is evidence of the exploit itself, and not of traffic to its endpoint. On matched controls it separates that exploit from the same request with a harmless value, and it raises no alerts across 27,081 legitimate and crawl requests. We never compile the exploit that produced the logs. Most are Splunk's public attack data, recorded by a third party. Without reading a single log, Encore's rules find 43 of the 45. Splunk's log-tested rules cover 30 of the 45, and Encore finds 28 of those, plus all 10 CVEs without an ESCU rule. Where Splunk's rules alert on 20 wrong CVE pairs, Encore's alert on only 2. Hunting can start as soon as a PoC is public, and rules can raise an alert when it provides a payload or host operation.
authors: Muhammad Shoaib; Alexander Suh; Joshua Andrew Tomiak; Wajih Ul Hassan

title: Kaynak Kod Güvenlik Açıklarının Tespiti, Açıklanması ve Giderilmesine Yönelik Çok Kipli Bir Yaklaşım
abstract: This thesis develops a multimodal approach to source code vulnerability detection, explanation, and mitigation. It investigates complementary software representations, including source code, general-purpose, security-aware, and taint-based metrics, together with functional and security-oriented summaries generated by large language models (LLMs). These representations are evaluated independently and through multimodal fusion using classical machine learning models, deep learning architectures, pretrained code models, and LLMs. The study also examines dataset quality, duplicate and near-duplicate samples, class imbalance, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness under semantic-preserving code transformations. The later stages extend vulnerability detection toward structured explanation and LLM-assisted mitigation. Multimodal evidence is used to generate explanations containing a vulnerability summary, the likely root cause, vulnerability mechanism, trigger conditions, a predicted Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) category, likely security consequences, and supporting evidence derived from source code, generated summaries, metric attributions, and detector alignment. These explanations guide candidate repair generation, while independent validation evaluates structural integrity, semantic alignment with the identified weakness, repair intent, and consistency with available security evidence. The selected components are integrated into VulAREL (Vulnerability Assessment, Repair, and Explanation across Learning Models), a traceable, function-level framework connecting multimodal detection, structured explanation, and candidate repair while separating generation from hidden-reference evaluation. The findings show that the value of multimodal evidence varies across tasks, datasets, and model families; explanation-guided mitigation is more effective than code-only mitigation; and generated repairs require independent validation and human oversight. Overall, the thesis provides a practical, auditable, and comprehensive framework for source code vulnerability analysis.
authors: İbrahim Tarakcı

title: A Layered Security Framework and Metrics for Analysing Cross-site Scripting Attacks
abstract: Single Page Applications (SPAs) have become a dominant architecture for modern client-side web systems by shifting state management, routing, and user interface processing to the browser. Although frameworks such as Angular provide built-in security mechanisms, including contextual escaping, template sanitization, and secure data binding, developers may introduce security weaknesses through practices such as unsafe DOM manipulation, dynamic script loading, and improper use of bypass mechanisms. Existing approaches to SPA security assessment primarily focus on identifying known vulnerability patterns through static analysis, providing limited insight into architectural security weaknesses and accumulated security complexity. This study contributes a Metrics-Driven Layered Security Framework (LSF) for assessing and improving the security architecture of Angular SPAs against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. The proposed framework organizes SPA security controls into three architectural layers: the Rendering Layer, Control Logic Layer, and Outer Shell Layer. It introduces seven security metrics, including Sanitization Bypass Density, Unmanaged Active Sink Frequency, Maximum Nesting Depth, Cyclomatic Branching Factor, CSP Policy Strictness Score, Boundary Validation Density, and Dependency Vulnerability Coefficient, which are combined into composite layer risk scores for comprehensive security assessment. The framework was empirically evaluated through controlled experiments involving Angular developers, comparing developers using the LSF-supported Layered Security Metrics Tool (LSMT) against developers performing unaided manual security reviews. The findings demonstrated that the proposed metrics and framework improve developers’ ability to identify structurally complex XSS-related weaknesses across Angular SPA security layers. The results demonstrate that the LSF provides a measurable approach for proactive vulnerability identification, architectural security auditing, and integration into Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) security processes.
authors: Nevy Kimani Maina; Geoffrey Muchiri Muketha; Jane Wanjiru Njuki

title: Making Small Code LLMs More Efficient for Secure Code Review with Neuro-Symbolic Fine-Tuning
abstract: As AI coding assistants generate more code, the need to review it for security flaws grows. Existing approaches leave a gap: static analyzers identify program sites but offer little explanation, while language-model explanations can be difficult to verify. Small open-weight code models could make security review available without sending proprietary code to a hosted service. We study whether fine-tuning helps these models turn security evidence into explanations that developers and tools can check. We present secSemScan, which pairs a static analyzer with a locally deployable model that writes a schema-constrained security monologue naming program sites, assigning a CWE, and giving a machine-parseable verdict. We also introduce OGSM (Oracle-Grounded Security Monologue), a dataset of 1,993 C/C\texttt{++} functions covering 22 CWEs in the taint and lifetime families. Each record pairs a function with analyzer-derived or fix-diff-derived evidence and a monologue. We fine-tune three open-weight code models in two stages, first on the output format and then on the monologue content. Because evaluation prompts supply the verdict and evidence, our results measure how well models use that information, not whether they detect vulnerabilities independently. On 355 test records, fine-tuning raised Qwen2.5-Coder-7B's verdict accuracy from 4.8\% to 96.6\%; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B reached 78.9\%, and StarCoder2-7B reached 43.7\%. Qwen2.5-Coder-7B cited 87.5\% of Tier~1 oracle sites, and every line it cited belonged to the oracle evidence. The results suggest that fine-tuning helps small models produce more structured, evidence-linked security reasoning.
authors: Mostafijur Rahman Akhond; Mahmuda Khatun; Gias Uddin

title: Enhancing Neural Code Representation With Additional Context
abstract: Automated program comprehension underpins many software engineering tasks, from code summarisation to clone detection. While recent deep learning models have achieved strong results, they typically rely on source code alone and overlook other information that developers routinely use to understand programs, such as version history or structural relationships. This gap limits the ability of current models to capture the broader context in which code evolves and operates. To address this, we conduct an empirical study of how enriching code representations with these additional contextual signals affects the performance of neural models on key program comprehension tasks. We evaluate four downstream software engineering tasks, code clone detection, code classification, code summarisation, and vulnerability detection, using SeSaMe (1,679 semantically similar Java methods from 11 open-source projects), CodeSearchNet (2,117 projects; 63,259 methods paired with natural-language documentation), and Vul4J (178 vulnerability-inducing methods). To ensure a robust comparison, we fine-tune five foundational code models (tree-based and pre-trained Transformer architectures), namely CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5, PLBART, and ASTNN, under both code-only and context-augmented settings. We further expand the evaluation to seven code-specialised large language models (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B/14B, and DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B), comparing prompt-based context injection against fine-tuned use of context. Experimental results show that context improves classification performance for all five foundational models and, after fine-tuning, for most of the seven LLMs. For summarisation, the effect depends on the model family: version history improves all four foundational models on every metric, whereas context injected into the prompt of a decoder-only LLM helps two of the seven models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B and 14B, via call-graph context) and lowers both lexical and semantic metrics for the other five. In particular, encoding version history never hurts and usually improves clone detection across the five foundational models (up to +15.92% F1 for CodeT5) and summarisation (e.g., GraphCodeBERT +5.56% METEOR; CodeT5 +3.05% BLEU-4). By contrast, call-graph context delivers model- and task-dependent gains. Combining multiple types of context (version history, call graphs, and method age) can further enhance improvements, reaching up to +21.48% macro-F1 in code classification and +15.04% F1 in clone detection for specific models under concatenation-based aggregation. Finally, a human evaluation with two annotators on 100 Java snippets (rank-ordering with ties evaluation) showed that context-augmented summaries were ranked significantly higher than summaries from models that rely on source code only for Accuracy and Content Adequacy (Wilcoxon \(p\leq 0.026\) ; Cliff's \(\lvert\delta\rvert\) up to 0.55), while improvements in Conciseness were context-dependent; inter-rater agreement was high (Kendall's \(\tau_{b}\) ). Our study highlights the potential benefit of utilising rich and diverse context to enhance the code comprehension capability of neural-based models. An exploratory evaluation on vulnerability detection provides initial evidence that context-enriched representations transfer to security-oriented tasks. It also opens new research directions for optimising contextual encoding strategies in software engineering, for instance automated bug localisation, where call-graph context helps trace fault propagation paths [68].
authors: Huy Gia Nguyen; Christoph Treude; Patanamon Thongtanunam
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

title: A Survey of LLM-based Software Repair: Taxonomies, Design Paradigms, and Applications
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping automated program repair. We present a reproducible hierarchical taxonomy that organizes 66 LLM-based repair systems according to where repair capability and control logic principally reside: taskadapted parameters, prompt and context design, designer-specified workflows, or LLM-directed runtime control. Adaptation, generation pattern, runtime control, and auxiliary evidence remain separate coded dimensions. This representation exposes control distinctions hidden by utilization labels and supports cross-paradigm analysis of system design and evaluation evidence. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first publicly available LLM-based software repair survey to operationalize Fine-Tuning, Prompting, Procedural, and Agentic as one corpus-wide primary classification. Our hierarchy complements prior surveys with a single corpus-wide primary decision rule, while the result-level protocol audit bounds which reported results are defensibly comparable. To analyze how repair systems use benchmarks, we record benchmark variants, metrics, base models, and fault-localization assumptions for each system’s primary reported result, identifying protocol-aligned comparison windows and benchmark-family fragments. We clarify paradigm trade-offs in task alignment, deployment cost, controllability, and multi-hunk or cross-file repair. We outline open challenges and research directions. Our artifacts and scripted survey pipeline are publicly available at https://github.com/GLEAM-Lab/ProgramRepair .
authors: Boyang Yang; Zijian Cai; Fenglin Liu; Bach Le; Lingming Zhang; Tegawendé François Bissyandé; Yang Liu; Haoye Tian
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

title: Chain-of-Thought Oversight Requires Separate Evidence for Faithfulness and Monitorability
abstract: A common assumption in chain-of-thought (CoT) oversight is that a visible reasoning trace makes model behavior easier to monitor. We argue that this assumption can conflate distinct properties along a chain linking a model's internal computation, reasoning artifacts, outputs, and monitor judgments. We identify four properties along this chain: reasoning visibility (whether a trace is accessible), mechanistic faithfulness (whether a trace reflects internal computation), mechanistic localizability (whether a compact causal mechanism can be isolated), and behavioral monitorability (whether a monitor can detect the target behavior). Two complementary case studies across three open-weight reasoning models show why these distinctions matter. In the security vulnerability reasoning study, probes and activation ablations provide evidence of internal representation and causal influence, but a monitor with access to the reference answer does not outperform the majority-class baseline in a held-out test. In authority-hint factual reasoning study, a monitor correctly distinguishes changed from unchanged answers, but seven mechanistic analyses do not isolate a compact causal mechanism. These results show that evidence for one claim does not establish the others. We therefore propose an evidential-chain reporting standard. Each claim carries a licensing statement that specifies its target property, access tier, and artifact, and labels each required link as supported, unsupported, or assumed. These assessments determine whether the conclusion is licensed, conditionally licensed, or not licensed.
authors: Sichao Li; Sai Ma; Xiyang Hu; Chudi Zhong; Tongliang Liu

title: Chakraview: A Hybrid Static-Analysis and Local-Llm Prototype for Vulnerability Detection and Mitigation Guidance in Open-Source Software
abstract: Open-source software benefits from rapid, distributed development, but reviewing it for security weaknesses is labour-intensive, and developers need findings that are explained and actionable. We present Chakraview, a prototype that combines a rule-based static stream with a locally hosted large language model (DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B Instruct served through Ollama). Uploaded Python, C/C++, PHP, and Java files or ZIP archives are parsed with Tree-sitter, analysed by both streams, fused by a weighted score (0.6 × LLM confidence + 0.4 × static flag), and reported with CWE labels, explanations, and suggested mitigations. We document the architecture, analyse the fusion rule, and report two preliminary checks: seven functional checks recorded in project documentation, and a reproducible measurement of the static stream on four developer-written files containing 29 seeded vulnerable lines, of which 23 were flagged (22 under the correct CWE); all misses were injection-type flaws needing data-flow reasoning. The LLM stream, the fusion score, and the generated fixes have not been evaluated on labeled data, and suggested fixes are not compiled, tested, or rescanned. Chakraview is therefore a preliminary system prototype, not a validated detector. We specify a held-out evaluation protocol comparing static-only, LLM-only, and fused analysis, with separate tests of localization, calibration, and mitigation correctness.
authors: Ajay Vinod Dawkhare Amit Rushikesh Tayade; Aryan Mandar Wable; Sakshi Sopan Bhor Mayur Shashikant Thakare
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to automate vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly, the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the harness: the code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static, improvements on one dataset or model may not transfer to others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each iteration, it searches over the history of prior harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for various architectures. A validation set (202 pairs) is used for optimization, while an unseen dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to others. We show that harnesses optimized with one model transfer to another, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.
authors: Ira Ceka; Arnav Garg; Ryan Lutz; Ting Zhang; Ratnadira Widyasari; Gail E. Kaiser; Baishakhi Ray

title: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction
abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
authors: Haoran Bu; Yiting Shen; Litian Zhang; Ruihan Hu; Xi Zhang

title: Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code
abstract: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether their code is readable, efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities, yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026), with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute, variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks, extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B. At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs. In the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal.
authors: Prashank Kadam

title: Scan Before You Install: Detecting and Mitigating Local and Composite Vulnerabilities in Skills
abstract: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.
authors: Parth A. Gandhi; Avital Aviv; Prasanna N. Wudali; Yuval Elovici; Asaf Shabtai

title: Structured Security Explanations for Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection
abstract: Software vulnerability detection remains difficult because existing approaches rely on predefined analysis rules, learn vulnerability patterns implicitly from code and labels, or use large language models (LLMs) to make the final security judgment. It remains unclear whether structured descriptions of security-relevant program behavior can improve supervised detection. We present VulnLens, an explanation-augmented framework for binary C/C++ vulnerability detection that separates program-behavior analysis from the final decision. A label-blind LLM-based Explainer examines each function from seven fixed perspectives: data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic and type behavior, control flow, shared state, and external-resource access. Without receiving vulnerability labels or CWE information, it generates structured explanations. A supervised Detector combines source code and explanations through sequential cross-attention. We evaluate VulnLens on a PrimeVul-derived dataset covering ten CWE categories and test transfer to SecVulEval without retraining. On the 526-function PrimeVul test set, VulnLens achieves 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, exceeding DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 percentage points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1. Matched explanations improve F1 by 7.3 points over a separately trained code-only detector. On SecVulEval, VulnLens achieves 66.4% accuracy and 65.8% F1, outperforming DeepSeek V4 Pro by 7.6 points in accuracy and 20.0 points in F1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 16.6 points in accuracy and 7.8 points in F1.
authors: Fares Trad; Yizhou Chen; Hung Viet Pham; Zeyu Sun; Gias Uddin

title: Artificial Intelligence for Security Analysis of Smart Contracts: A Systematic Review
abstract: This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) investigates the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for smart contract vulnerability detection in Web3 decentralized applications (dApps). Smart contracts enable trustless finance, decentralized governance, and autonomous economic protocols; however, their immutability makes vulnerabilities deployed on-chain difficult to patch without costly governance interventions. Between 2020 and 2024, 127 high-impact attacks caused $2.3 billion in cumulative losses, while state-of-the-art automated tools could have prevented only 8% of them (10 of 127, $149M). Following PRISMA guidelines, records retrieved from IEEE Xplore, the ACM Digital Library, and Springer Link were screened, resulting in 93 primary studies selected for in-depth analysis. The review organizes the literature around three generations of AI-based detection: classical machine learning, deep learning and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and Large Language Models (LLMs). The findings show that LLM-based detectors often achieve high recall but limited precision, while GNNs obtain strong results on narrowly scoped economic attacks, such as sandwiching, but still struggle to generalize. Logic-layer and protocol-layer vulnerabilities, which account for a significant share of financial losses, remain insufficiently addressed. The review also highlights emerging directions, including cross-contract reasoning, automated repair, and the security implications of the post-quantum cryptography transition. Persistent challenges include dataset scarcity, limited explainability, weak generalization, and the lack of robust methods for complex cross-contract and protocol-level vulnerabilities. These insights provide guidance for future research toward more accurate, explainable, and comprehensive AI-based security analysis of smart contracts.
authors: Lívia Carrera; Raquel Coelho Gomes Pinto; Anderson Fernandes Pereira dos Santos
venue: Brazilian Symposium on Multimedia and the Web

title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
abstract: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.
authors: Mostafijur Rahman Akhond; Mahmuda Khatun; Gias Uddin

title: CIVER: Causal Intervention Verification for Reliable Code Review
abstract: Code review is essential for maintaining software repositories by identifying defects, improving code quality, and supporting reliable software evolution. With the growing adoption of LLM-based coding agents, an increasing number of code contributions and repository changes are generated by these agents. Consequently, LLM-based code review agents are becoming increasingly prevalent to evaluate these contributions and maintain software quality. However, LLM reviewers often generate lengthy reviews containing numerous potential issues, many of which are false positives or lack sufficient evidence. These unreliable reviews can mislead developers and downstream coding agents, motivating the need to distinguish actionable findings from unsupported claims. We propose CIVER, a causal intervention-based framework that identifies the core issues underlying code-review findings and distinguishes genuine defects from false positives. CIVER integrates three modules: a review module assesses findings, an intervention module generates repair-oriented perturbations, and a verifier module scores review reliability. Through joint optimization via expert iteration, the three modules identify genuine defects by responding to targeted repairs while remaining stable under unrelated changes. Extensive experiments on SWE-Review-Bench demonstrate that CIVER correctly identifies 77% of genuine defects through targeted repairs. Cross-project and downstream repair evaluations further demonstrate that CIVER generalizes across repositories and improves coding agents' task success rates, highlighting its effectiveness for reliable automated code review.
authors: Xinyuan Song; Hasibul Haque; Jay Somasundaram; Ryan Turner; Bowen Zhu; Liang Zhao

title: Governed Retrieval Augmented Generation with Guardrails Role Based Access Control and Audit Logging
abstract: Enterprise retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must preserve source permissions while controlling unsafe content and retaining audit evidence. This paper integrates permission-tagged ingestion, authorization-aware retrieval, guardrails, and correlated logging, and evaluates the authorization boundary in a reproducible synthetic diagnostic. Five retrieval strategies were compared across eight corpus randomizations, each containing 750 documents, 12 principals, and 360 queries under five policy conditions. SQLite FTS5 supplied exact lexical ranking; no language model or Amazon Bedrock deployment was evaluated. Indexed filtering alone admitted unauthorized context in an average 99.5% of role-revocation queries and 57.7% of document-revocation queries. Adding a current-permission recheck produced zero observed context violations in the tested conditions. With 10% of private index metadata removed, authorized recall was 92.1%; policy-service outages forced all protected methods to abstain. An independent recomputation verified the saved retrieval and policy decisions. These results illustrate a known stale-permission failure mode and its mitigation under a trusted policy model. They do not establish production security, generated-answer safety, or regulatory compliance.
authors: Lohith Reddy Kalluru
venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.
authors: Zirui Ding; Xinxin Fan; Hao Yuan; Shaoye Luo; Men Niu; Quanliang Jing; Yunfeng Lu

title: Trajectory-Level Security Debt in LLM Coding Agents
abstract: LLM coding agents can traverse hundreds of intermediate code states before submitting a solution. Evaluating only the final artifact leaves the evolution of security findings unmeasured. We introduce the Security Debt Line Integral (SDLI), which accumulates static-analysis risk when an agent reaches a new best test pass ratio. We instantiate it with four static application security testing (SAST) tools and study artifacts from 830 passing SWE-bench runs, 712 ProgramBench final workspaces, and 13 public MirrorCode trajectories. The two large populations use the final-state special case of SDLI. Two-tool Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) class agreement occurs in 3.9% of SWE-bench runs and 26.2% of the 80 ProgramBench runs passing at least 90% of official tests. These are scanner findings, not validated vulnerability rates. Excluding three advisory-heavy classes reduces the latter rate to 6.2%. Same-task runs differ in their measured scores, while one reconstructed ProgramBench run exposes persistent findings from its first implementation write. A repair case study reduces the scanner signal while preserving tested behavior, but also reveals sensitivity to equivalent API rewrites. SDLI offers a way to study progress and security findings together. Its value for steering agents and confirming exploitable vulnerabilities remains to be established.
authors: Prateek Kumar Rajput; Abdoul Kader Kaboré; Yewei Song; Melissa Tessa; Tyler Malloy; Jacques Klein; Tegawendé François Bissyandé
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

title: YATA: AN EXPLOIT-VERIFIED MULTI-AGENT FRAMEWORK FOR AUTONOMOUS DETECTION AND REPAIR OF WEB APPLICATION VULNERABILITIES
abstract: Security scanners are good at raising alarms and poor at proving them: they over-report and under-report, and a human must still reproduce each alert, write a patch and decide the application is safe.Large language models can now draft such patches almost for free, but a confidently written wrong patch is hard to catch, and the same models are increasingly able to exploit real applications, so trusting a model's verdict only moves the risk.This paper presents YATA (Yet Another Threat Antagonist), a multi-agent framework that works backward from evidence: a weakness is reported only after an exploit has actually run against the code, and a patch is kept only after the framework's own offensive engine re-attacks itwith the original payload and with mutated variantsand fails.Six agents (HUNTER, HEALER, VALIDATOR, MUTATOR, LEARNER, REPORTER) cover source code in Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, while a separate engine, RECON, applies the same discipline to live web targets over HTTP.Every model call carries a deterministic fallback, so the system runs fully offline.On nineteen seeded repositories spanning nine vulnerability classes, YATA proved and repaired all twenty planted vulnerabilities and blocked all 71 mutated payloads, with zero model calls.
venue: International Journal of Progressive Research in Engineering Management and Science

title: NeuroGraph: an AI graph-driven neuro-symbolic framework for explainable threat reasoning in advanced manufacturing
abstract: Abstract The growing complexity of cyber-physical attack surfaces in advanced manufacturing environments has made reliable cyber threat intelligence analysis increasingly challenging. While large language models and retrieval-augmented generation have enhanced cyber threat intelligence capabilities, text-based approaches remain prone to hallucinations and lack structured reasoning over interconnected threats. Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation partially addresses this limitation but often fails to support ontology-consistent multi-hop reasoning and transparent evidence tracing across heterogeneous cybersecurity knowledge. This paper proposes a graph-grounded neuro-symbolic framework that integrates ontology-aware symbolic query generation, knowledge graph retrieval, and neural language generation to enable accurate and explainable threat analysis across information technology and operational technology domains. The proposed framework employs a dual-large language model architecture in which the first model translates natural-language queries into executable Cypher statements for symbolic graph retrieval, while the second generates responses exclusively from the retrieved graph evidence. Experimental evaluation on publicly available cyber threat intelligence benchmarks demonstrates consistent improvements over the published baseline in reasoning accuracy while reducing hallucinations, improving multi-hop reasoning, and increasing robustness against adversarial perturbations. Runtime and explainability analyses further show that the framework maintains interactive inference performance while exposing graph-grounded reasoning artifacts that enable analysts to inspect and verify each stage of the reasoning process. These results demonstrate the potential of graph-grounded neuro-symbolic reasoning to provide scalable, interpretable, and reliable cyber threat intelligence for next-generation Industry 5.0 environments.
authors: Padmeswari Nandiya; Ahmad Mohsin; Iqbal Hasan Sarker; Ahmed Ibrahim; Helge Janicke

title: From Shadow IT to Shadow AI: A Scoping Review of How Embedded AI and Employee Use Increase Cybersecurity and Data Privacy Risk
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into enterprise software has introduced a critical governance challenge: Shadow AI, the unmanaged and often invisible adoption of AI tools and features by employees outside formal IT oversight. Unlike traditional Shadow IT, which centers on unauthorized data storage and infrastructure, Shadow AI operates at the knowledge and decision-making layer, introducing probabilistic risks including data leakage, agentic misalignment, and indirect prompt injection that existing security frameworks are ill-equipped to address. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) synthesizing 38 peer-reviewed and industry sources to investigate three research questions: how organizational visibility gaps into embedded and employee-used AI increase cybersecurity and data privacy risk; what cybersecurity incident types are most commonly associated with ungoverned AI-enabled applications; and what risks employee interactions with AI pose to sensitive, proprietary, and regulated data. The analysis identifies a critical visibility deficit created by AI capabilities embedded within vendor-managed platforms, the semantic opacity of large language model interactions, and employees' utilitarian bypass of security policies. A taxonomy of six AI-specific incident types is presented, encompassing data leakage, prompt injection, credential compromise, agentic misuse, phishing augmentation, and insecure plugin exploitation. Findings demonstrate that existing governance mechanisms, including data loss prevention systems, identity and access management frameworks, and static risk assessments, are structurally misaligned with the dynamic nature of generative AI. The paper recommends a transition to dynamic, risk-based governance integrating continuous monitoring, cross-functional oversight, and AI TRiSM frameworks.
authors: Jenny Ahn; Bogdan Pavlyuchenkov; Lasette Smith; Paul Wagner; Robert J Honomichl; Ryan Straight; Shengjie Xu
venue: Journal of Cybersecurity Education Research and Practice

title: A Hybrid Feature Fusion Framework for Just-in-Time Software Defect Prediction using LLM Reasoning and CodeBERT Embeddings
abstract: Abstract Just-in-Time (JIT) software defect prediction tries to flag risky commits the moment they are committed, before they can cause problems in a codebase. Most existing approaches rely on simple change metrics, such as how many lines were added or how experienced the developer is, but these numbers say very little about what a change actually does. This paper presents a hybrid framework that looks at a commit from three angles at once: traditional change metrics, a semantic understanding of the code from CodeBERT, and structured reasoning about intent and risk generated by a large language model. We built a multi-language dataset of nearly 60,000 commits from 19 open-source Java, Python, and C/C++ projects, and tested several ways of combining these three sources of information using standard machine learning classifiers. Combining traditional metrics with CodeBERT's code understanding consistently gave the strongest results, clearly outperforming any single source used alone. Adding the LLM-based reasoning on top of that combination did not meaningfully improve things further, though it was genuinely useful when paired with either of the other two sources on its own. Overall, our results suggest that combining structural and semantic information is a practical way to catch defects early, while a third, coarser reasoning layer adds little once the first two are already working together.
authors: K. Panimozhi; Pratham K P; Pratheeksha Pai; Sachin Kumar E

title: Cumulative and Audited Guardrail Tool Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in open-world environments where safety risks cannot be fully predefined. However, most existing guardrail mechanisms remain static, relying on fixed rules, prompts, or classifiers that generalize poorly to emerging risks. Here we present EVOLVE, a tool-level self-evolving defense framework that formulates agent security as a process of cumulative security evolution. Inspired by how human societies transform experiences into transferable protective knowledge, EVOLVE externalizes security knowledge into executable guardrail tools that are continuously inherited, independently audited, and iteratively refined through lifelong interaction. Across multiple benchmarks, backbone models, and embodied environments, EVOLVE consistently outperforms existing defenses across diverse risk scenarios with +22\% average F1 score. We further validate the framework in real-world robotic and autonomous agent systems. Our results suggest that scalable agent safety may require continuously evolving defense systems rather than static guardrails.
authors: Xiao Yang; Aishan Liu; Siyuan Liang; Zonghao Ying; Le Wang; Jiakai Wang; Xianglong Liu; Dacheng Tao

title: Fixed Detectors, Moving Code: How Well Do Static Security Analyzers Hold Up over a Decade of C/C++ Evolution?
abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools are often deployed on the assumption that detectors configured today will remain effective on future code, including previously unknown vulnerabilities. We test this assumption using 20,000 vulnerable and fixed C/C++ cases from 1,116 open-source projects (2016-2025), evaluated with three CodeQL releases, three Infer releases, and one Semgrep configuration. To distinguish temporal effects from shifts in code composition, we compare yearly populations, project- and label-matched year pairs, and within-project trajectories. We investigate the largest within-project declines through repair diffs, detection predicates, alert locations, and execution logs, while accounting for failed, degraded, and costly analyses. Under changed-file case-label scoring, overall F1 ranges from 0.066 to 0.478, but count-based AUROC stays near chance (0.495-0.526). Newer CodeQL releases attain higher F1 alongside nearly parallel rises in recall and false-positive rate, not stronger separation of vulnerable from fixed cases. In project-matched year pairs, CodeQL R2024 has negative mean later-minus-earlier F1 at every source-year gap, whereas Infer v1.1 and v1.3 have positive means throughout. Among selected drops, only 6 of 39 CodeQL and 2 of 620 Infer findings overlap a changed repair line. For Semgrep, 78.96% of cases show parser or timeout diagnostics even though every run reports success. These results suggest that apparent changes in temporal SAST effectiveness can arise from broader alerting, changing analysis coverage, and incidental findings, not solely from losses in vulnerability detection. Evaluations of temporal sustainability should fix detector conditions, control for projects, inspect repair-level evidence, and report failed or degraded analyses.
authors: Jun-Hua Tang; Zhengsong Zhang. Haipeng Cai

title: AI-Powered Penetration Testing and Vulnerability Remediation for GitHub Repositories
abstract: AI-Powered Penetration Testing and Vulnerability Remediation for GitHub Repositories presents PentestAI, a web platform that scans a developer's GitHub repositories for security vulnerabilities, verifies the serious findings in an isolated sandbox and proposes fixes as pull requests.The system combines a Large Language Model (Google Gemini) that analyses the most securityrelevant source files with a deterministic pattern-matching pass that detects committed secrets such as API keys and private keys.High and critical findings are re-checked with CodeQL and Semgrep inside network isolated Docker containers to reduce false positives.A fixer service generates a patch with a code model, re-scans the patched code twice and opens a pull request only if the vulnerability is gone and no new issue is introduced.The application is built with TanStack Start, React and Supabase, and supports weekly automated scans, vulnerability lifecycle tracking, reports and an AI security assistant.The results show that the platform turns a manual, expensive security audit into a fast, repeatable and verifiable process for everyday developers.
authors: Mrs. Bindu K.P; Gagana R; Kushal K R; M G Sahana; M Harshit Pramod

title: Reinforcement Learning for Software Vulnerability Analysis: A Systematic Review with Emphasis on C/C++ Source Code and Static Analysis
authors: Bruno Caro-Vásquez; Carola Figueroa-Flores; Gastón Márquez

title: A Review of Source Code Vulnerability Detection Methods Based on Large Language Models: Models, Techniques, and Evaluation
abstract: In source code vulnerability detection, large language models (LLMs) are no longer used only as substitutes for traditional fixed classifiers. With prompt design, parameter fine-tuning, and program-context information, they can judge whether code contains vulnerabilities and can also provide suspicious locations and explanatory evidence. This paper takes lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models as two main lines of discussion. It reviews methods for input construction, task adaptation, the use of program-analysis information, and multi-model collaboration, and compares them in terms of datasets, evaluation metrics, and deployment conditions. Existing studies show that code pretraining, prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and structural-information enhancement can improve detection or explanation results on specific benchmarks. However, such improvements are easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions, which may lead to overestimated performance. Therefore, model evaluation should not rely on a single metric alone. It should also report the data source, detection granularity, temporal or project-level isolation, false-positive cost, and whether generated explanations can be verified by program evidence. On this basis, this paper further discusses an application approach centered on data governance, strict data splitting, uncertainty calibration, and SAST-LLM-human collaboration. The discussion is limited to source-code-level vulnerability detection, localization, and classification, and does not cover network intrusion detection, malware analysis, smart-contract-specific detection, vulnerability generation, or automatic repair.
authors: Letong Qin

title: The Landscape of Static-Analysis Optimizations
abstract: This paper presents the first Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of optimization techniques for static analyses, a fundamental method for detecting vulnerabilities and defects early in software development without executing code. Despite its effectiveness, static analysis faces challenges such as false warnings and high computational demands on large code bases. Prior research has demonstrated that performance can be significantly enhanced through techniques such as staging, sparse analysis, and parallelization. However, a systematic assessment of these techniques, their goals, and their interactions is still lacking, often limiting their broader impact. To map the landscape of static-analysis optimizations, we reviewed 146 research papers published between 2009 and 2025, categorizing them into a methodology-based taxonomy. This paper discusses specific optimization goals and examines the potential benefits of combining techniques from multiple categories. We find that most optimizations primarily target efficiency (time and memory), while few studies aim to improve precision. Most publications propose single techniques, with only a third combining multiple approaches. Optimizations predominantly target pointer analysis, though many are likely more broadly applicable. Other common targets include call-graph construction, taint analysis, and data-flow analyses. While some combinations, such as demand-driven and incremental analysis, have proven effective, others—such as staging and procedure summaries—remain under-explored, indicating significant potential for synergistic optimizations.
authors: Palaniappan Muthuraman; Leen Jubarah; Aashish Prajapati; Rose Sunil; Vaibhav Chaudhari; Eric Bodden
venue: ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
abstract: A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it.
